name: Resonance
kicker: Big vibrations at a natural frequency · How a well-timed push lifts a swing
dates: Studied in sound by Hermann von Helmholtz, 1860s
briefing: Every swing, guitar string, wine glass, and bridge has a natural frequency at which it likes to vibrate. Push it again and again at exactly that rhythm, and the vibrations grow bigger and bigger: that’s resonance. It is why a well-timed push sends a swing soaring, why a powerful singer can shatter a wine glass with one loud note, and why engineers add dampers to keep tall buildings and bridges from swaying dangerously.
answerHtml: Resonance (accept word forms like resonant or resonating; prompt on natural frequency or sympathetic vibration)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: London’s Millennium Bridge closed two days after it opened in 2000, when walkers’ footsteps fell into step with its sideways sway and made it wobble more and more. Engineers fixed that bridge by adding dampers, devices that soak up the energy of this effect.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect in which a system vibrates more and more strongly when it is pushed at its natural frequency.

tossups.p: The 1940 collapse of the Tacoma Narrows Bridge, nicknamed “Galloping Gertie,” is often blamed on this effect, although engineers say the true cause was a related twisting motion called aeroelastic flutter. That bridge in Washington State twisted wildly in a steady wind just four months after it opened.
tossups.r: This effect lets a well-timed push send a playground swing higher and higher. For 10 points, name this effect, in which a system is driven at its natural frequency.

tossups.p: England’s Broughton Suspension Bridge, near Manchester, collapsed in 1831 while a column of soldiers marched across it in step. Afterward, the British Army began ordering troops to break step when crossing bridges, to avoid this effect.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, in which repeated pushes at an object’s natural frequency make its vibrations grow larger and larger.

tossups.p: Daniel Kirkwood found gaps in the asteroid belt where an asteroid would circle the Sun, for example, exactly three times for every one orbit of Jupiter, a gravitational case of this effect. Saturn’s moon Mimas [“MY-mus”] helps clear the Cassini Division in Saturn’s rings in the same way.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, which also lets a singer shatter a wine glass by singing its natural pitch.

tossups.p: Hermann von Helmholtz used hollow spheres with two openings, each built to respond to a single pitch, to pick out the notes hidden inside a sound through this effect. Blowing across the top of an empty bottle makes it hum by the same effect.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect that lets a powerful singer shatter a wine glass by matching its natural frequency.

tossups.p: Turning a radio’s tuning dial adjusts a circuit of an inductor and a capacitor so that this effect happens at the frequency of just one station. In such a circuit, energy sloshes back and forth between the inductor and the capacitor at their natural rate.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, in which a system responds strongly to pushes at its own natural frequency.

tossups.p: A system’s “Q factor” tells how sharp and long-lasting this effect is, so a high-Q tuning fork rings for a long time after it is struck. Damping, such as friction, lowers and widens the peak on a graph of this effect.
tossups.r: The letter R in MRI stands for a magnetic form of this effect. For 10 points, name this effect, in which a system vibrates strongly at its natural frequency.

tossups.p: Quartz watches keep time with a tiny crystal that vibrates 32,768 times per second, the rate at which this effect makes the crystal ring most strongly when an electric circuit pushes on it. That number is two to the fifteenth power.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, in which pushing an object at its natural frequency makes it vibrate strongly, as when a swing is pushed in rhythm.

tossups.p: The “ocean” you hear when you hold a seashell to your ear is really background noise boosted by this effect inside the shell’s hollow space. The hollow body of an acoustic guitar uses this effect to make the strings’ sound louder.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, in which an object vibrates strongly when pushed at its natural frequency.

tossups.p: In a classic lab, students hold a humming tuning fork over a tube of water and raise or lower the water until the sound suddenly gets loud, showing this effect in the air column. Striking one tuning fork can make an identical fork nearby start humming on its own.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, in which a system vibrates especially strongly when pushed at its natural frequency.

tossups.p: The Taipei 101 skyscraper hangs a giant steel ball near its top as a tuned mass damper, which sways against the building to fight this effect during typhoons and earthquakes. Tall buildings are designed so that their natural sway does not match the shaking they are likely to face.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect in which a system shakes harder and harder when pushed at its natural frequency.

tossups.p: A sitar has extra strings that the player usually leaves unplucked; they ring by this effect when the played strings sound their notes. Holding down a piano’s sustain pedal and singing loudly into the piano makes its strings answer back by the same effect.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, in which vibrations at an object’s natural frequency make it vibrate strongly.

tossups.p: The vowel sounds of human speech come from peaks called formants, which this effect creates in the throat and mouth. Changing the shape of your mouth changes which pitches this effect boosts, which is how you can tell an “ee” from an “oo.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, which lets a singer break a wine glass with the right note.

tossups.p: Pluto circles the Sun twice for every three orbits of Neptune, and Jupiter’s moons Io, Europa, and Ganymede are locked in a 1:2:4 pattern; both are orbital examples of this effect. The pattern between Pluto and Neptune keeps the two from ever coming close, even though their orbits seem to cross.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, in which a swing goes higher when pushed in rhythm with its natural frequency.

tossups.p: Cesium atomic clocks keep time by adjusting microwaves until cesium atoms respond most strongly, at a rate of about 9.19 billion vibrations per second that has defined the second since 1967. Your ear canal boosts sounds near 3,000 hertz by the same effect.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, which lets a well-timed push send a child on a swing higher.

trap.title: Effect, not frequency
trap.body: Resonance is the effect; the natural (or resonant) frequency is just the special frequency at which it happens, so “natural frequency” earns only a prompt and plain “frequency” is wrong. Clues about strings, organ pipes, and tuning forks can also tempt players into “harmonics” or “standing waves,” and a siren’s changing pitch is the Doppler effect, not this.
trap.fix: Vibrations that grow from well-timed pushes, shattered wine glasses, swings, swaying bridges, dampers, and tuned radios mean resonance. The special frequency itself is the natural frequency; patterns of nodes on a string are standing waves; and a moving source’s pitch shift is the Doppler effect.
trap.line: Real answer line: Resonance (accept word forms like resonant or resonating; prompt on natural frequency or sympathetic vibration)
